And this, beyond the popular protest, is also creating a standoff within the armed forces.” ; Explained that the 25 senior army leaders had, before the corps meeting, clearly decided over seven days of meetings that they are obedient servants of the government, and that they walked out of the assembly when a position statement was tabled declaring the Tigray interim administration an enemy that must be dissolved so the legally empowered TPLF takes over.

a6217.speaker: Gebru Asrat, veteran Arena party politician and former TPLF fighter
a6217.name: Gebru Asrat
a6217.title: veteran Arena party politician and former TPLF fighter
a6217.speech: Notes that Shaebia too is supporting this movement of the military leaders and suggests that the TPLF of Debretsion (Dr) wishes to operate in alliance with Shaebia if possible ; Notes that the federal government too believes the interim administration is weak, mentioning that former Minister of Defence Abraham Belay (Dr) also confirmed this recently ; “The TPLF of Debretsion (Dr) and the group of military leaders it has assembled also has a desire to work together with Shaebia. It is trying this in practice, and beyond that it has become known that it has begun efforts to form an alliance with Amhara forces in order to march on Addis Ababa. And Shaebia is known to be a force that is also allied with Egypt”, adding that the matter is a tension that goes beyond Tigray and threatens the country.

a6217.speaker: Gebru Asrat, veteran Arena party politician and former TPLF fighter
a6217.name: Gebru Asrat
a6217.title: veteran Arena party politician and former TPLF fighter
a6217.speech: Explains that Tigray’s political chaos has created multifaceted problems, and indicated that the tension the military officers have created will, starting from creating a civil war in Tigray, also create a new tension in the alignment of forces with Shaebia, the federal government and other forces ; Says the TPLF’s old cadres and the military officers gathered around them do not want the accountability and demand for change coming in Tigray, and that keeping the old political line intact has become a matter of life and death for them ; Shared his worry that if the army digs in insisting the TPLF must remain in power the Tigray crisis will enter a dire condition, and indicated that his Arena party, other opposition parties, civic associations and pro-change forces have taken the position that a new inclusive interim administration should be established in Tigray.

a6217.speaker: Abraham Belay (Dr), former Minister of Defence
a6217.name: Abraham Belay (Dr)
a6217.title: former Minister of Defence
a6217.speech: Recently confirmed that the federal government believes the Tigray interim administration is weak (as cited by Gebru Asrat).

a6217.speaker: Redwan Hussein (Ambassador), one of the government’s main negotiators at Pretoria
a6217.name: Redwan Hussein (Ambassador)
a6217.title: one of the government’s main negotiators at Pretoria
a6217.speech: Explaining at the time how the agreement was signed, indicated that although the agreement document contained a provision that no armed force other than the federal security forces could operate in Tigray, the federal government, in good faith and on the grounds that it would benefit the people of Tigray, gave the authority to maintain the region’s peace to the Tigray security forces themselves ; Said at a meeting with opposition political organisations a few days after the signing that government representatives, in open discussion with the TPLF’s military and political leaders at Pretoria, agreed it would be better for the Tigray security force itself, rather than the federal defence forces, to take over Tigray’s security.

a6217.speaker: Redwan Hussein (Ambassador), the government’s negotiator
a6217.name: Redwan Hussein (Ambassador)
a6217.title: the government’s negotiator
a6217.speech: Explained in detail that although the agreement said the defence forces would take full control of security work, the decision was taken in good faith and by mutual understanding, because it was agreed that full deployment of the defence forces and disarmament of Tigrayan fighters would, beyond making Tigray’s political forces appear utterly defeated, harm the psychology of the people of Tigray and the next rounds of political negotiation, and would not bring lasting peace.

a6217.speaker: Debretsion Gebremichael (Dr), TPLF chairman and former president of the Tigray region
a6217.name: Debretsion Gebremichael (Dr)
a6217.title: TPLF chairman and former president of the Tigray region
a6217.speech: In his own law, Proclamation No. 365/2015, stipulated that government structures, including the security force, are under the regional government.

a6217.speaker: Group of Debretsion Gebremichael (Dr) / TPLF head office (statement of Megabit 27, 2016 E.C. and general assembly)
a6217.name: Group of Debretsion Gebremichael (Dr) / TPLF head office (statement of Megabit 27
a6217.title: 2016 E.C. and general assembly)
a6217.speech: Accused the interim administration, saying “it is working to weaken the army and transform itself into a military order”, and called for action to be taken ; At the TPLF general assembly, called for the army to take action against the leaders under the interim administration who ‘trade in its name’ and to hand power over to the legal TPLF.

a6217.speaker: Getachew Assefa (Dr), Tigray political analyst resident in Canada
a6217.name: Getachew Assefa (Dr)
a6217.title: Tigray political analyst resident in Canada
a6217.speech: Says that the Brigade Nhamedu meeting in Addis Ababa is an indicator that there are war preparations between Ethiopia and Eritrea.

a6217.speaker: Getachew Assefa (Dr), Tigray political analyst resident in Canada
a6217.name: Getachew Assefa (Dr)
a6217.title: Tigray political analyst resident in Canada
a6217.speech: “The relationship between Shaebia and the TPLF gives much to think about. In 1977 E.C. it was Shaebia that prevented the people of Tigray from finding a way out of the famine. Its differences with the TPLF are deep-rooted. Nevertheless, there are still people in the TPLF today who feel absolute submission to Shaebia. It was one month before the Tigray war began that Shaebia’s people wrote a document about the attack they would carry out on Tigray... The Shaebians are making good use of the division of Tigray’s political elites. Everything inside Tigray is decided by Shaebia... The Shaebians, having committed all that destruction on Tigray, find it astonishing to think that the people of Tigray will still stand by their side and support them in fighting the Ethiopian government they call the enemy. No one attempts this except those within the TPLF who are utterly subservient to Shaebia,” he explained to Reyot Media.

a6217.speaker: Semhal Meles, daughter of the late former Prime Minister Meles Zenawi (English-language article, ‘Tigray Military Forces: Partial Arbitrator of Conflict?’)
a6217.name: Semhal Meles
a6217.title: daughter of the late former Prime Minister Meles Zenawi (English-language article, ‘Tigray Military Forces: Partial Arbitrator of Conflict?’)
a6217.speech: Notes that no force has emerged that is equally acceptable both to the people of Tigray and to the federal government, and tries to show that the struggle to be found acceptable in both directions is one origin of the dispute ; Says that alongside the disagreement created by the signing, ownership and implementation of the Pretoria peace agreement, differences over the interim administration’s independence and decision-making authority and over party interference also contribute to the split ; States that the Tigray army, having long wavered between the two groups, has in the end confirmed that it stands with Debretsion (Dr) and the TPLF head office, and details that this could bring a severe crisis for the region.

a6217.speaker: Semhal Meles, daughter of the late former Prime Minister Meles Zenawi
a6217.name: Semhal Meles
a6217.title: daughter of the late former Prime Minister Meles Zenawi
a6217.speech: Says that given the existential dangers Tigray has faced, the continuation of the split and the erosion of Tigray’s unity brings additional grave danger ; Says the Prosperity government will continue to aggravate Tigray’s problem and fan the fire, and notes that the Election Board has been dragging out — including by issuing a proclamation — its response to the demand that the TPLF’s legal recognition be restored ; Says various delays are being carried out so that the constitutional order is not restored in Tigray, no election is held for the region to form its own government, and it has no representatives in the federal parliament and the House of Federation, underlining that this frustrates not only the democratic order but the effort to build a multinational federal country.

a6217.speaker: Semhal Meles, daughter of the late former Prime Minister Meles Zenawi
a6217.name: Semhal Meles
a6217.title: daughter of the late former Prime Minister Meles Zenawi
a6217.speech: “Prime Minister Abiy’s (Dr) government will not determine the way it handles the conduct of the Tigray army without properly examining the nature of its relationship with the new Donald Trump administration. During Trump’s earlier term, America’s relationship with Ethiopia hung solely on the favourable attitude Vice President Mike Pence had towards Ethiopia. And Prosperity benefited greatly from this. Be that as it may, Donald Trump is not a leader who has a policy option for African countries, which he insults as filthy. There is no certainty about what his relationship with African countries such as Ethiopia will be based on in his second term. At a time when the violation of international law and order, as well as territorial expansionism, are taking root, the global acceptability of liberalism and capitalism has fallen into danger. Within this global reality, will the Tigrayan elites in whose hands the fate of the people of Tigray lies continue, as they have always done, as promoters of neoliberal politics cloaked in revolutionary democracy, or will they join the political camp that says change and reform should come first? That is a matter to be awaited” ; Says that unless Tigray’s elites seek political solutions that match the changing international political situation and withstand the dangers that have arrived, the existence of the people of Tigray will fall into grave danger.

a6217.speaker: Proclamation No. 359/1995 (law on federal intervention in regional affairs)
a6217.name: Proclamation No. 359/1995 (law on federal intervention in regional affairs)
a6217.speech: Stipulates that the federal government and the House of Federation have a high responsibility towards a region in which an interim administration has been established; Article 16 stipulates the submission of reports and follow-up and Article 17 sets out informing the public; it stipulates that the Prime Minister shall regularly submit his report and follow-up assessment to the House of Federation every two months and shall appear whenever members ask for an explanation, and that the government and the House of Federation must give explanations to the media.

a6253.speaker: Tiffany Miller, US Embassy's Acting Deputy Chief of Mission
a6253.name: Tiffany Miller
a6253.title: US Embassy's Acting Deputy Chief of Mission
a6253.speech: “These donations include a second five-bed ICU in Otjiwarongo, as well as two field hospitals in Outapi and Katima Mulilo that include a 30-bed Negative Pressure Isolation Facility and a UN Level 1 Urgent Care Clinic. These donations will total over N$128 million in value and represent the largest single humanitarian assistance donation to date to the Namibian people.”

a6253.speaker: Ben Nangombe, Executive Director, Ministry of Health and Social Services
a6253.name: Ben Nangombe
a6253.title: Executive Director, Ministry of Health and Social Services
a6253.speech: Says the ministry discovered during the COVID-19 pandemic that there were only 23 ICU beds in public hospitals across Namibia: “With the installation of ICU capacity here, it means that instead of having to refer patients from here to Windhoek, they can be treated here. There is a risk when you have to transport a patient who needs ICU care, put them in an ambulance that is not fully adequate, and send them on a long trip on a bumpy road. Anything can happen there, so the best is to provide the service locally, and that's what we are trying to do here with the donation.”

a6253.speaker: Ben Nangombe, Executive Director, Ministry of Health and Social Services
a6253.name: Ben Nangombe
a6253.title: Executive Director, Ministry of Health and Social Services
a6253.speech: Indicated that the mobile ICU will further boost the skills and knowledge of the workforce as they decentralise the service to the patients.

a6292.speaker: Dr Nguéto Tiraïna Yambaye, Director General of the African Guarantee and Economic Cooperation Fund (Fagace)
a6292.name: Dr Nguéto Tiraïna Yambaye
a6292.title: Director General of the African Guarantee and Economic Cooperation Fund (Fagace)
a6292.speech: “The African continent is potentially rich but chronically underfinanced, because classical banking institutions are cautious in granting productive credit.”

a6292.speaker: Dr Nguéto Tiraïna Yambaye, Director General of Fagace
a6292.name: Dr Nguéto Tiraïna Yambaye
a6292.title: Director General of Fagace
a6292.speech: “Our interventions are 80% directed at SMEs,” he explains, recalling that Fagace sets up guarantee lines and supports project promoters in drawing up their business plans. “Our role is to push banks to contribute to development, particularly in the sectors they often avoid, such as agriculture and livestock,” he insists.

a6292.speaker: Jules Ngankam, Director General of the African Guarantee Fund (AGF) Group
a6292.name: Jules Ngankam
a6292.title: Director General of the African Guarantee Fund (AGF) Group
a6292.speech: “Despite the internationally recognised importance of SMEs, small African businesses face difficulties in accessing financing for their growth and innovation needs” ; “AGF is the missing link that allows banks to carry out their SME financing strategies effectively.”

a6292.speaker: World Bank, World Development Indicators 2024
a6292.name: World Bank
a6292.title: World Development Indicators 2024
a6292.speech: Cited as the source that bank deposits represent, on average, less than 20% of GDP in several West African countries, compared with more than 40% in Asia or Latin America.

a6292.speaker: Abdourahmane Diallo, Director General of the African Solidarity Fund (FSA)
a6292.name: Abdourahmane Diallo
a6292.title: Director General of the African Solidarity Fund (FSA)
a6292.speech: “Determined, committed and responsible, the Fund is striving to build together, with its partners, a better and sustainable future.”

a6292.speaker: African Development Bank (AfDB/Bad)
a6292.name: African Development Bank (AfDB/Bad)
a6292.speech: Cited as the source that SMEs make up more than 80% of Africa's economic fabric.

a6292.speaker: World Bank, Global Findex 2025
a6292.name: World Bank
a6292.title: Global Findex 2025
a6292.speech: Cited as the source that about 58% of adults in sub-Saharan Africa had a bank or mobile money account in 2024, compared with 34% in 2014.

a6312.speaker: Edicts of the Secretariat-General of the Government of the Province of Cape Verde, 10 February 1876 (Official Bulletin no. 7/1876)
a6312.name: Edicts of the Secretariat-General of the Government of the Province of Cape Verde
a6312.title: 10 February 1876 (Official Bulletin no. 7/1876)
a6312.speech: The document included a map of all the city's urban axes (squares, small squares, streets and alleys), presenting their names in two columns, the "old names" and the "modern names"; in its "modern" toponymy the space came to be called "largo do Sá da Bandeira."

a6312.speaker: Luísa Reis Lima (1992, pp. 211-226), study
a6312.name: Luísa Reis Lima (1992
a6312.title: pp. 211-226), study
a6312.speech: According to her interpretation, the tradition of naming streets, squares and small squares persisted over time in analogous situations across the Portuguese world.

a6312.speaker: António Correia e Silva (1998, p. 53), study
a6312.name: António Correia e Silva (1998
a6312.title: p. 53), study
a6312.speech: Alludes to the "cemetery" adjacent to the Church, attesting to this location.

a6312.speaker: Minutes of the session of 6 August 1874 of the Praia Council
a6312.name: Minutes of the session of 6 August 1874 of the Praia Council
a6312.speech: Reported a plot behind the Town Hall, where at the time the Council's premises were to be enlarged; attention was drawn to the need to take into account the measurement of the graves in the foundation works to be carried out at that site.

a6312.speaker: Chelmicki (1821, pp. 70-72), study
a6312.name: Chelmicki (1821
a6312.title: pp. 70-72), study
a6312.speech: Identified the place, at the time, as an open site close to the church where the dead were buried.

a6312.speaker: Santa Rita Vieira (1993, p. 26), study
a6312.name: Santa Rita Vieira (1993
a6312.title: p. 26), study
a6312.speech: Refers to the Hermitage in these terms: "(...) a hermitage in which the Holy Virgin was venerated under that invocation and which was still to be seen at the beginning of the eighteenth century at the foot of the hill of the site."

a6364.speaker: Elsbeth Akkerman, Ambassador of the Kingdom of the Netherlands
a6364.name: Elsbeth Akkerman
a6364.title: Ambassador of the Kingdom of the Netherlands
a6364.speech: present at the event stated that “the Dutch Government’s development strategy is based on the following pillars: Sustainable Development, Gender Equality, Youth Support, Food Security, Water and Climate and all of them are clearly aligned with the development strategy of the Government of Mozambique”.

a6364.speaker: Mike Marchington, Director of Finance & Planning, Gorongosa Restoration Project (GRP)
a6364.name: Mike Marchington
a6364.title: Director of Finance & Planning, Gorongosa Restoration Project (GRP)
a6364.speech: On behalf of the GRP, Mike Marchington stated that “the Program we launched today is yet another affirmation of our commitment to combine conservation and community development. Biodiversity protection, to be successful, must be an inclusive process, with the participation of all, where community participation must result in tangible benefits for them, making communities the greatest guardians of the ecosystem. Finally, we want to state that, as a team, we are committed to the objectives of this program and to the rational use of the resources allocated to the SLDP by the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands”.

a6364.speaker: Stella da Graça Pinto Zeca, Secretary of State for the Province of Sofala
a6364.name: Stella da Graça Pinto Zeca
a6364.title: Secretary of State for the Province of Sofala
a6364.speech: At the end of the ceremony, the Secretary of State for the Province of Sofala affirmed the Government’s commitment to the success of the Program, recognizing that the Program is part of the Government’s Plan and the Sustainable Development Objectives of the United Nations that the Government of Mozambique has ratified.

a6430.speaker: Dr. Salah Banoita Tourab, Secretary General of the Djiboutian Ministry of Health
a6430.name: Dr. Salah Banoita Tourab
a6430.title: Secretary General of the Djiboutian Ministry of Health
a6430.speech: Stated at the closing ceremony: "more than 222,292 people have received at least one dose of the COVID-19 vaccine since the launch of the immunization campaign, a vaccination coverage rate of 42.51%, of which 66.71% are men and 33.29% women."

a6605.speaker: Parliamentary Select Committee on Sanitation and Water Resources of Ghana
a6605.name: Parliamentary Select Committee on Sanitation and Water Resources of Ghana
a6605.speech: Lauded Zoomlion Ghana Limited for its outstanding contributions to improving sanitation infrastructure and waste management in the country, following a working visit to the company's Accra Compost and Recycling Plant (ACARP) at Adjen-Kotoku on Wednesday, April 23, 2025.

a6605.speaker: John Oti Bless, Chairman of the Parliamentary Select Committee on Sanitation and Water Resources, MP for Nkwanta North
a6605.name: John Oti Bless
a6605.title: Chairman of the Parliamentary Select Committee on Sanitation and Water Resources, MP for Nkwanta North
a6605.speech: “I am truly impressed by the level of investment that has gone into these major companies,” he told journalists after the tour. “Zoomlion's infrastructure and operations are not only impressive but evidence that the capacity to manage Ghana's sanitation challenges already exists.”

a6605.speaker: John Oti Bless, Chairman of the Parliamentary Select Committee on Sanitation and Water Resources
a6605.name: John Oti Bless
a6605.title: Chairman of the Parliamentary Select Committee on Sanitation and Water Resources
a6605.speech: Lamented the government's failure to meet its financial obligations to service providers, revealing that the state currently owes Zoomlion over GH₵1.2 billion in arrears. “How can a company function effectively without resources?” he questioned. He indicated that the Ministry of Finance has earmarked GHS 13 billion in the 2025 budget to settle debts owed to sanitation service providers and expects swift action.

a6605.speaker: John Oti Bless, Chairman of the Parliamentary Select Committee on Sanitation and Water Resources
a6605.name: John Oti Bless
a6605.title: Chairman of the Parliamentary Select Committee on Sanitation and Water Resources
a6605.speech: Advocated for the establishment of a dedicated sanitation fund, arguing that a fixed percentage of the sanitation and energy levy should be channelled into sanitation improvement. “Sanitation is a daily necessity that requires a dedicated source of funding. If 40 pesewas is being raised through the levy, 20 pesewas should go to sanitation.”

a6605.speaker: John Oti Bless, MP for Nkwanta North
a6605.name: John Oti Bless
a6605.title: MP for Nkwanta North
a6605.speech: Called for enhanced public education, media partnerships, and enforcement of local sanitation bye-laws. “Many district assemblies' bye-laws are not gazetted, making them unenforceable,” he explained. “We need to fix this and work with the media to launch nationwide campaigns to educate the public.”

a6605.speaker: John Oti Bless, Chairman of the Parliamentary Select Committee on Sanitation and Water Resources
a6605.name: John Oti Bless
a6605.title: Chairman of the Parliamentary Select Committee on Sanitation and Water Resources
a6605.speech: Praised Zoomlion's innovation, particularly its ventures into local production of tricycles, furniture, and waste processing systems. “We urge Ghanaians and civil society to support and buy local products from Zoomlion. This fight is about public health, not politics” ; “We have hit the ground running, and we will not stop until the right things are done.”

a6605.speaker: Joseph Siaw Agyepong, Executive Chairman of the Jospong Group
a6605.name: Joseph Siaw Agyepong
a6605.title: Executive Chairman of the Jospong Group
a6605.speech: In an earlier presentation, called on Parliament to ensure strict enforcement of sanitation and environmental bye-laws. “What we do here goes beyond just cleaning,” he said. “We are tackling cholera, environmental degradation, and even enhancing tourism, all while improving sanitation infrastructure.”

a6605.speaker: Joseph Siaw Agyepong, Executive Chairman of the Jospong Group
a6605.name: Joseph Siaw Agyepong
a6605.title: Executive Chairman of the Jospong Group
a6605.speech: Appealed to the government to consider reducing import taxes on essential sanitation equipment. “The work we do often lacks the recognition and support it deserves,” he lamented. “We are currently in discussions about taxes on some of our equipment, and we urge the committee to take up this matter” ; “With the right backing, we can achieve much more in improving Ghana's sanitation landscape.”

a6613.speaker: Capterio (building on the World Bank's 2024 global gas flaring tracker and the International Energy Agency's 2024 global methane tracker)
a6613.name: Capterio (building on the World Bank's 2024 global gas flaring tracker and the International Energy Agency's 2024 global methane tracker)
a6613.speech: Reported that oil companies flared approximately 267 billion cubic meters of gas in a year, wasting about $48 billion in potential revenues globally.

a6613.speaker: Working paper on CSR funds from mining companies
a6613.name: Working paper on CSR funds from mining companies
a6613.speech: Found that CSR funds from mining companies in the DRC, Guinea, Sierra Leone, and Zambia disproportionately benefit local elites.

a6613.speaker: 2022 research study on Shell's CSR in Ogoniland
a6613.name: 2022 research study on Shell's CSR in Ogoniland
a6613.speech: Found out that Shell's CSR spent millions on clean-ups and infrastructure projects that had minimal direct impact in Ogoniland but mostly benefitted the local elites behind the scenes. The study concluded that the pro forma version of CSR permitted companies to amplify success while environmental damage and community grievances persisted.

a6613.speaker: African Digital Rights Network (ADRN)
a6613.name: African Digital Rights Network (ADRN)
a6613.speech: Reports that tech giants spend less than 4% of global research and development (R&D) in Africa, considering the continent's massive user base and data extraction.

a6613.speaker: African Development Bank
a6613.name: African Development Bank
a6613.speech: Warning of a potential $39.84 billion shortfall in Official Development Assistance projections for 2025.

a6613.speaker: UN Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA)
a6613.name: UN Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA)
a6613.speech: According to UNECA, closing Africa's infrastructure gap requires up to $170 billion annually.

a6738.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a6738.name: John Dramani Mahama
a6738.title: President of Ghana
a6738.speech: the promise President John Dramani Mahama made to uncap the NHIF in the 2025 budget.

a6738.speaker: Kwabena Mintah Akandoh, Minister of Health of Ghana
a6738.name: Kwabena Mintah Akandoh
a6738.title: Minister of Health of Ghana
a6738.speech: said the increase in budget allocation to the NHIA was in fulfillment of the promise President John Dramani Mahama made to uncap the NHIF in the 2025 budget. He said in 2024, the amount the formula allocated was around GH₵6 billion and as a result of the uncapping, GH₵10 billion had been allocated to the Fund.

a6738.speaker: Kwabena Mintah Akandoh, Minister of Health of Ghana
a6738.name: Kwabena Mintah Akandoh
a6738.title: Minister of Health of Ghana
a6738.speech: said the difference would cater for about three main items, including free primary healthcare, to fill the huge funding gap due to withdrawal of donor support to the health sector ; On the withdrawal of the support by the country’s donor partners, such as the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), he said it had created a huge funding gap in the health sector. “Therefore, revenue to be generated as a result of uncapping the NHIF will go to fill the gap,” the Health Minister said ; Under the free primary healthcare, he said any Ghanaians who fell sick could seek free medical treatment in any health centre.

a6738.speaker: Kwabena Mintah Akandoh, Minister of Health of Ghana
a6738.name: Kwabena Mintah Akandoh
a6738.title: Minister of Health of Ghana
a6738.speech: He recalled that in the 2024 formula, the government allocated GH₵2 million for dialysis treatment of people with renal issues below the age of 18 years and above the age of 60 years. “That formula died on December 31, 2024; so, beyond that there was no policy in place for dialysis. Now, with this formula what we have done is to include dialysis as part of the benefit package of the National Health Insurance Scheme just like malaria or any other disease. So, the policy direction is that we are going to fund the dialysis issues in this country,” he said.

a6738.speaker: Kwabena Mintah Akandoh, Minister of Health of Ghana
a6738.name: Kwabena Mintah Akandoh
a6738.title: Minister of Health of Ghana
a6738.speech: said a percentage would finance the Ghana Medical Trust Fund, Mahama Cares initiative, and that Mahama Cares would be dedicated to chronic non-communicable diseases. “And so any of these diseases that have not been captured by NHIF will then be captured by the Mahama Cares because we all know that about 45 per cent of our mortality is attributable to the non-communicable diseases, and as a country, we need to urgently find a solution to it, especially at this critical time where our donor partners are withdrawing their funds,” Mr Akandoh stated.

a6859.speaker: Emma Theofelus, Member of Parliament and Deputy Minister of Information, Communication and Technology (Namibia)
a6859.name: Emma Theofelus
a6859.title: Member of Parliament and Deputy Minister of Information, Communication and Technology (Namibia)
a6859.speech: Said women face gender biases in legal and macroeconomic frameworks, including young professionals in the informal sector. “Africa’s demographic dividend is very much dependent on the full inclusion of women across overlapping political, social and economic spheres.” She said this has far-reaching implications like limited opportunities to funding from commercial banks, trust from potential clients, fewer employees, as well as lower sales and annual turnover, furthermore constraining young women from starting, operating and scaling up enterprises.

a6859.speaker: Emma Theofelus, Deputy Minister of Information, Communication and Technology (Namibia)
a6859.name: Emma Theofelus
a6859.title: Deputy Minister of Information, Communication and Technology (Namibia)
a6859.speech: Added that narrowing the digital divide will ensure women fully participate in the 4th Industrial Revolution and have access to economic opportunities online. “Women have, in the past, been deliberately excluded from all the first three industrial revolutions. The opportunities availed by technology today cannot be ignored; the continent needs to take deliberate actions to ensure no young person is unable to use technology today.”

a6859.speaker: Emma Theofelus, Member of Parliament (Namibia)
a6859.name: Emma Theofelus
a6859.title: Member of Parliament (Namibia)
a6859.speech: Said that for Africa to develop, there needs to be gradual less reliance on the West, through foreign aid that has failed to deliver sustainable economic growth on the continent; she is advocating for more intra-Africa trade to alleviate poverty amongst other things.

a7025.speaker: Peter Mutharika, President of Malawi
a7025.name: Peter Mutharika
a7025.title: President of Malawi
a7025.speech: Vowed to root out government corruption and rebuild an ailing economy after he was sworn in for a second term; in his inaugural address he said his administration was inheriting a country in economic crisis, facing acute food shortages, cost-of-living pressures, and a lack of foreign exchange that has crippled businesses and led to persistent fuel shortages ; “There is no money in government. Borrowing is extremely high, and nobody knows where the borrowed money has gone.”

a7025.speaker: Peter Mutharika, President of Malawi
a7025.name: Peter Mutharika
a7025.title: President of Malawi
a7025.speech: Pledged improvements, saying: “We will fix this country.” ; “I don't promise you milk and honey. I promise you hard work, tough and painful decisions” ; “The honeymoon of looting government is over!”

a7025.speaker: Peter Mutharika, President of Malawi
a7025.name: Peter Mutharika
a7025.title: President of Malawi
a7025.speech: Appealed to the international community for investment and addressed U.S. President Donald Trump directly, saying he would soon send a delegation to America to discuss his country's prospects, especially after cuts in U.S. foreign aid.

a7025.speaker: Malawi Congress Party (statement)
a7025.name: Malawi Congress Party (statement)
a7025.speech: Said in a statement that although the outgoing president Lazarus Chakwera was absent from the inauguration, he wished Mutharika success and good health.

a7025.speaker: Malawi Government (@MalawiGovt, social media post)
a7025.name: Malawi Government (@MalawiGovt
a7025.title: social media post)
a7025.speech: “President of Mozambique Daniel Chapo, Zimbabwean President Emerson Mnangagwa, Tanzanian Prime Minister Kassim Majaliwa, are some of the foreign guests attending the Inauguration and swearing in ceremony of President Professor Arthur Peter Mutharika Vice President Jane Ansah”.

a7052.speaker: Tewodros Zewdu, Director General of the Ethiopian Horticulture Producers and Exporters Association
a7052.name: Tewodros Zewdu
a7052.title: Director General of the Ethiopian Horticulture Producers and Exporters Association
a7052.speech: Explains that although more than half a billion dollars in foreign exchange is currently being earned from the sector, this is small relative to Ethiopia's potential; said the country has a wide opportunity to increase its annual foreign exchange earnings from the sector four- or five-fold but has not been able to take advantage of it, and that if the bottlenecks were removed more than one billion dollars a year could be earned, adding that the association can present concrete data supporting this.

a7052.speaker: Tewodros Zewdu, Director General of the Ethiopian Horticulture Producers and Exporters Association
a7052.name: Tewodros Zewdu
a7052.title: Director General of the Ethiopian Horticulture Producers and Exporters Association
a7052.speech: Pointed out that there are many indications of Ethiopia's opportunity in the sector, citing as examples that while production costs are rising globally Ethiopia has better production costs, and adding that the favourable conditions Ethiopian Airlines offers for exporting Ethiopian products internationally are also seen as a good opportunity.

a7052.speaker: Tewodros Zewdu, Director General of the Ethiopian Horticulture Producers and Exporters Association
a7052.name: Tewodros Zewdu
a7052.title: Director General of the Ethiopian Horticulture Producers and Exporters Association
a7052.speech: Said there are numerous challenges preventing flower, vegetable and fruit exports from advancing to the desired level, citing first of all problems with land supply as an obstacle to investors expanding their investments, and adding that the breakdown of peace and security and power interruptions have also held the sector back ; Asked whether farms had closed or pulled out because of insecurity, indicated that although some companies had stopped operating most are continuing to work while withstanding the challenges, noting that the one said to have ceased operations is a single company with two farms ; Said any investment goes where there is peace and a better profit margin, and that since the damage to horticulture from insecurity is clearly visible, investors are forced to work while bearing many challenges ; Said reliable and lasting peace is necessary for workers to work with peace of mind and that the clusters in particular face serious challenges which must be put right.

a7052.speaker: Tewodros Zewdu, Director General of the Ethiopian Horticulture Producers and Exporters Association
a7052.name: Tewodros Zewdu
a7052.title: Director General of the Ethiopian Horticulture Producers and Exporters Association
a7052.speech: Raised the limited infrastructure of refrigerated warehouses, vehicles and container supply as another crucial point needing resolution, citing examples: the world's second-largest shipping company exported about seven thousand containers from Kenya but only 40 from Ethiopia, 38 from Somalia and 280 from Tanzania, while the shipping company MCC loaded about 800 refrigerated containers but only ten from Ethiopia, most of them avocado; said that since refrigerated containers, warehouses and related services contribute greatly to competitiveness in the world market this service must be started on a wide scale, while also noting that Ethiopian Airlines' refrigerated cargo service has made it possible to be competitive in flower exports.

a7052.speaker: Tewodros Zewdu, Director General of the Ethiopian Horticulture Producers and Exporters Association
a7052.name: Tewodros Zewdu
a7052.title: Director General of the Ethiopian Horticulture Producers and Exporters Association
a7052.speech: Indicated that in order to solve the problem of land supply the government should resolve this bottleneck by preparing land for the sector on the basis of study.

a7052.speaker: Ethiopian Horticulture Producers and Exporters Association
a7052.name: Ethiopian Horticulture Producers and Exporters Association
a7052.speech: Announced that, together with an international company called HHP, it will hold the ninth Horti Flora Expo from Megabit 23 to 25, 2017 (Ethiopian calendar), with more than 140 companies and visitors from more than 40 countries participating.

a7052.speaker: Tewodros Zewdu, Director General of the Ethiopian Horticulture Producers and Exporters Association
a7052.name: Tewodros Zewdu
a7052.title: Director General of the Ethiopian Horticulture Producers and Exporters Association
a7052.speech: Said such an exhibition also contributes to Ethiopia's industry and is not only a business forum but one at which nine different panel discussions will be held that can carry Ethiopia's horticulture industry forward ; Said previous exhibitions created new markets and that, since purchase agreements are concluded there, the country will gain a great deal; recalled that earlier exhibitions contributed greatly to Ethiopian horticultural products entering various countries, including markets such as Korea and Japan in addition to the regular European market, and played a large role in entering the African market.

a7052.speaker: Dokram Stock, Director of HHP
a7052.name: Dokram Stock
a7052.title: Director of HHP
a7052.speech: Said that research papers showing international experiences in the horticulture sector, including recommendations indicating what Ethiopia should do, will be presented and discussed alongside the exhibition ; Said that the companies attending the exhibition being internationally renowned companies in the sector will help to further modernise Ethiopia's horticulture sector, that since extensive preparation has been made and various buyers will also participate it will greatly help in promoting Ethiopian products and generating new buyers, and that well-known experts in the sector will also take part in the panel discussions.

a7076.speaker: UN World Health Organization (WHO)
a7076.name: UN World Health Organization (WHO)
a7076.speech: Said eight countries - six of them in Africa, including Nigeria, Kenya and Lesotho - could soon run out of HIV drugs following the US government's recent decision to pause foreign aid.

a7076.speaker: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO chief
a7076.name: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus
a7076.title: WHO chief
a7076.speech: Warned that “Disruptions to HIV programmes could undo 20 years of progress” ; added it could also lead to more than 10 million additional cases of HIV and three million HIV-related deaths, noting this was “more than triple the number of deaths last year” ; said at a press conference on Monday that Nigeria, Kenya, Lesotho, South Sudan, Burkina Faso and Mali - as well as Haiti and Ukraine - would run out of life-saving anti-retroviral (ARV) medicines in the coming months ; said the disruption has led to the “immediate stop to services for HIV treatment, testing and prevention in more than 50 countries”.

a7076.speaker: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO chief
a7076.name: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus
a7076.title: WHO chief
a7076.speech: “The US administration has been extremely generous over many years. And of course, it's within its rights to decide what it supports and to what extent” ; “But the US also has a responsibility to ensure that if it withdraws direct funding for countries, it's done in an orderly and humane way that allows them to find alternative sources of funding.” ; “We ask the US to reconsider its support for global health, which not only saves lives around the world, it also makes the US safer by preventing outbreaks from spreading internationally.”

a7076.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a7076.name: Donald Trump
a7076.title: US President
a7076.speech: Announced the freeze on foreign aid on his first day in office in January as part of a review into government spending; his executive order paused foreign aid support for an initial duration of 90 days in line with his “America First” foreign policy; he also announced during his first days in office that the US would pull out of the WHO.

a7076.speaker: WHO data
a7076.name: WHO data
a7076.speech: Cited as the source that Kenya has the seventh-largest number of people living with HIV in the world, at around 1.4 million.

a7095.speaker: Donald Trump, President of the United States
a7095.name: Donald Trump
a7095.title: President of the United States
a7095.speech: Announced the cutting of USAID funds to Africa.

a7095.speaker: Efraim Shimbali, Namibia YALI 2024 Partnership and Resources Mobilisation Coordinator (opinion author)
a7095.name: Efraim Shimbali
a7095.title: Namibia YALI 2024 Partnership and Resources Mobilisation Coordinator (opinion author)
a7095.speech: Argues that while the aid cut was a devastating moment filled with panic for many African countries, it "exposes a tentative failure of African leadership" and lay bare how Africans are dependent on America and the external community ; Writes that colonialism was a system of creating the continent's dependence on the colonisers, that Africa's constant waiting for donated medicines and funds makes it "akin to a street beggar", and that Africans ought to decolonize themselves and produce within the continent what the international community provides ; Argues Africa's economy is still defined by the second Industrial revolution, exporting raw materials and importing expensive finished products, and that any aid should be for the transfer of skills and machinery rather than final products or monetary funds ; Argues Africa needs to decolonise and improve its education system, which tests linguistic ability instead of teaching people to identify and solve community problems and to invent and produce, citing Namibia's Cambridge-accredited system three decades after independence ; Concludes: "I think Trump should really cut these aid packages to Africa to loosen the mental slavery of the African leadership and help Africans to think of fighting for total independence on their continent", adding that the international community will never teach decolonisation because it created and benefits from the system of dependence.

a7199.speaker: Zimbabwean business community
a7199.name: Zimbabwean business community
a7199.speech: Reacted coolly to the 18 percent tariff regime imposed on Zimbabwe by the US, saying it would have minimal impact on the economy as trade between the two countries was low, weighed down for decades by Washington's unilateral sanctions.

a7199.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a7199.name: Donald Trump
a7199.title: US President
a7199.speech: Claiming unfair trade practices against Washington by the rest of the world, slapped varying tariffs on virtually all countries around the globe, to even out trade.

a7199.speaker: A prominent local businessman (anonymous - declined to be named for fear of being placed on Western travel restrictions)
a7199.name: A prominent local businessman (anonymous - declined to be named for fear of being placed on Western travel restrictions)
a7199.speech: "What was once an adversity, today it is a silver lining." ; "Imagine what the impact could have been had our trade with the outside world still be configured in the patterns of the 1980s and 90s where the West dominated."

a7199.speaker: Tapiwa Marimo, Confederation of Zimbabwe Retailers acting chief executive
a7199.name: Tapiwa Marimo
a7199.title: Confederation of Zimbabwe Retailers acting chief executive
a7199.speech: "This situation underscores the need for Zimbabwe to diversify its export markets and enhance local production to cushion the economy from such external shocks." ; warned that "The imposition of an 18 percent tariff by the United States on Zimbabwean exports is likely to strain the country's trade performance and contribute to a decline in exports."

a7199.speaker: 2023 trade statistics between Zimbabwe and the United States (latest available)
a7199.name: 2023 trade statistics between Zimbabwe and the United States (latest available)
a7199.speech: According to the statistics, Zimbabwe exported goods worth US$119 million to the United States, versus imports of US$45 million; much of Zimbabwe's exports was made of ferrochrome, raw tobacco and sugar, while imports mainly consisted of tractors, sorghum and vegetable oils.

a7296.speaker: Joyce Keston, 47, Cyclone Freddy survivor and vice-chairperson of Mtemangawa Village Development Committee, Nsanje District
a7296.name: Joyce Keston
a7296.title: 47, Cyclone Freddy survivor and vice-chairperson of Mtemangawa Village Development Committee, Nsanje District
a7296.speech: “Today, our fertile farmland is buried in sand and rocks, no longer favourable for food production,” says the mother of four. “Water points were also damaged.” ; “Our land is no longer usable” ; “With Cyclone Jude last month, we didn't feel it much because of the dyke, though it only covers a part of the village due to funding gaps.”

a7296.speaker: Post-disaster assessments
a7296.name: Post-disaster assessments
a7296.speech: Keston was among the 3.8 million people affected by acute food insecurity caused by flooding, post-disaster assessments show.

a7296.speaker: Jemina Phiri, Churches Action in Relief and Development (Card) district projects coordinator
a7296.name: Jemina Phiri
a7296.title: Churches Action in Relief and Development (Card) district projects coordinator
a7296.speech: Says communities equipped to adapt to climate change are better prepared to withstand the onset of climate-related disasters. “Considering the massive loss and damage, we provided them with cash and technical knowledge on how to build a dyke. This is besides training them to manage village savings and loans so they adapt to climate change challenges.”

a7296.speaker: Department of Disaster Management Affairs (Dodma)
a7296.name: Department of Disaster Management Affairs (Dodma)
a7296.speech: According to Dodma, Cyclone Freddy affected over 2.2 million people across the Southern Region, leaving 2,500 dead and hundreds still missing. Dodma estimates the loss and damage at $506 million, with about $680 million required for recovery and reconstruction.

a7296.speaker: Climate change experts
a7296.name: Climate change experts
a7296.speech: Say African countries are losing five to 15 percent of their GDP to climate change, erasing years of progress. This costs developing economies over $525 billion.

a7296.speaker: Participants at the 4th African Regional Conference on Loss and Damage in Lilongwe
a7296.name: Participants at the 4th African Regional Conference on Loss and Damage in Lilongwe
a7296.speech: Proposed strategies for accelerating mobilisation and access to climate finance for impactful locally led loss and damage and adaptation.

a7296.speaker: Julius Ng'oma, national coordinator of the Civil Society Network on Climate Change
a7296.name: Julius Ng'oma
a7296.title: national coordinator of the Civil Society Network on Climate Change
a7296.speech: To Ng'oma, the Loss and Damage Fund established in 2023 at CoP28 demonstrated a commitment to addressing un-adaptable and unmitigated climate impacts. “We want developed countries to provide more climate financing to deal with losses and damages because their gas emissions contribute to effects of climate change, which we Africans experience.” ; Ng'oma says activating the Santiago Network on Loss and Damage would ensure developing countries report and account for loss and damages requiring action.

a7296.speaker: Charles Mwangi, Pan-African Climate Justice for Action head of programmes and research
a7296.name: Charles Mwangi
a7296.title: Pan-African Climate Justice for Action head of programmes and research
a7296.speech: Asks multilateral financial institutions to simplify access to climate finance without conditionalities that hinder African countries from tapping the much-needed resources. “They should also establish a fair and transparent climate finance architecture that ensures direct access for frontline communities and prevents the dominance of intermediaries that slow down or misallocate funds.”

a7296.speaker: Joyce Keston, Cyclone Freddy survivor, Nsanje District
a7296.name: Joyce Keston
a7296.title: Cyclone Freddy survivor, Nsanje District
a7296.speech: “We want such funds to be in the form of grants and should be directly given to affected communities for speedy handling of adaptation programmes in our areas.”

a7296.speaker: Fenella Frost, United Nations Development Programme resident representative
a7296.name: Fenella Frost
a7296.title: United Nations Development Programme resident representative
a7296.speech: Urged Malawi to embrace strategic resource mobilisation and utilisation, including capacity building.

a7296.speaker: Owen Chomanika, Minister of Natural Resources and Climate Change
a7296.name: Owen Chomanika
a7296.title: Minister of Natural Resources and Climate Change
a7296.speech: Says there is a need to explore untapped climate financing avenues, including domestic and private contributions, as African countries struggle to access global funds due to harsh loan conditions. “For years, we have left the private sector out of our climate finance discussions and yet they are an important player sector in bringing climate solutions. We need to concretize discussions on the best approach for enhancing collaboration with the private sector on climate change management.”

a7296.speaker: Communique released at the Lilongwe conference
a7296.name: Communique released at the Lilongwe conference
a7296.speech: Calls for a global shield to upscale support to African countries facing existential threat to loss and damage. They also petitioned for flexible financial support for country-driven, needs-based climate solutions.

a7501.speaker: Financial Times
a7501.name: Financial Times
a7501.speech: has announced that the 12th edition of its flagship Africa Summit will take place in London on October 21-22, 2025, under the theme "Africa in a Changing World", bringing together African Heads of State, policymakers, CEOs, investors, and next-generation entrepreneurs.

a7501.speaker: Financial Times (statement)
a7501.name: Financial Times (statement)
a7501.speech: "The dramatic changes to America's foreign policy in Donald Trump's second term and his upending of the decades-old global trading system present challenges, uncertainties and risks for Africa as other outside powers intervene" ; the FT notes there may also be opportunities if Africa can pivot toward trade and investment over aid.
